cards.title: G. Ratta
cards.sub: 1994 · Bellcore · chief editor, ATM Forum UNI 3.1
cards.prompt: UNI 3.1 arrived a year after UNI 3.0 and its own draft lists every section it changes. Traffic control is not one of them. So who designed the policer the 1994 spec prints, and where does the spec say so?
cards.answer: The ITU did. UNI 3.1 states on the page that Figure 3-15 is a generic version of Figure 1 in Annex 1 of I.371, and that I.371's T and tau have been relabelled increment I and limit L because the algorithm now gets used in several places. The Forum named and generalised it; it did not invent it.
cards.body: Ratta ran the edit, not the design. His preface gives the mandate in one clause - align the Forum's implementation agreements with international standards - and the draft adds that it reflects only the changes to UNI 3.0 needed for that: signalling, OAM, management. Section 3.6 is untouched, so the rate limiter is inherited text.

cards.title: Policing a customer who obeyed
cards.prompt: A carrier discards cells from a connection that never exceeded its contracted rate, and the specification says in advance that this will happen. What physically happened to those cells between the customer's shaper and the policer?
cards.answer: Multiplexing clumped them. Cells of one connection are held while cells of another are inserted at a multiplexer's output, so a perfectly spaced stream arrives bunched and trips the tolerance limit at the UNI even though the source obeyed the contract.
cards.body: The spec concedes it: a usage parameter controller may take policing actions on a compliant connection, discarding more cells than were actually non-conforming. The remedy offered is not a fix — safety margins may be provisioned to limit the degradation. The discards are booked against network performance. No price is put on them.

cards.title: Figure 3-15
cards.prompt: Name the 1994 document and figure that prints one rate-limiting test as two different algorithms, and give the one-line identity the spec uses to prove they are the same limiter.
cards.answer: ATM Forum UNI 3.1, section 3.6.2.4.1, Figure 3-15 — itself a generic version of Figure 1 in Annex 1 of ITU-T I.371. The identity: at every arrival epoch, once both have run, TAT = X + LCT.
cards.body: Left flowchart: virtual scheduling, advancing a theoretical arrival time. Right flowchart: a continuous-state leaky bucket, a real-valued counter draining at one unit per time unit. The spec is explicit that the algorithm depends only on two parameters, an increment and a limit, and that the bucket's capacity is their sum.

cards.title: srTCM
cards.prompt: Five years after UNI 3.1 the IETF needed a policer for Diffserv. What metering structure did RFC 2697 specify, and what does that structure tell you about which half of the ATM traffic contract survived the move to IP?
cards.answer: Two token buckets, C and E, sharing one rate CIR — the GCRA's rate-plus-tolerance pair renamed as CIR, CBS and EBS. The algorithm survived intact; per-flow signalling, admission control and the negotiated contract around it did not.
cards.body: Six pages, Informational, September 1999. It marks each packet green, yellow or red against a committed rate and two burst sizes. The string ATM appears in it zero times. This is the shape now sitting in the rate limiter of every API gateway you will ever configure.
